title: Signalized kernel benchmarking: TRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graph sync issues
next_steps: Redwood to share per-kernel NVTX trace and condensed cudagraph replay logs
Customer to send representative 512/2k prompt set and a small traffic replay
Schedule on-prem pilot sync for week of 2027-09-13
action_items: Maya Liu: upload kernel-level NVTX traces + a short how-to on filtering (due 2027-09-07)
Marcus Li: provide VM spec and sample traffic config (due 2027-09-08)
Diego Ramos: run quantization sensitivity test (int8) on Catalyst's 7B model and share delta metrics (due 2027-09-10)
header:
Date: 2027-09-03 10:30 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Sanjay Patel, Maya Liu, Diego Ramos (Redwood) / Eve Torres, Marcus Li, Priya Natarajan, Tom Becker (CatalystAI)
summary: Deep technical session comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM kernel behaviors under realistic traffic with CUDA graph replay. Discussed persistent KV cache implications, eviction behavior, nonblocking cudagraph replay causing tail latency spikes, and tradeoffs for a private VPC deployment. Agreed to exchange traces and run on-prem pilot with representative workload.
topics: kernel selection heuristics (matmul tiling, fused attention paths)
CUDA graph capture/replay nondeterminism and sync points
KV cache eviction/persistence across batched requests
Quantization sensitivity (int8 vs int4) and perf/accuracy tradeoffs
Batching strategies for mixed short/long prompts
VPC/on-prem constraints: NIC, numa, and kernel affinity
questions: What causes intermittent tail latency even with steady QPS?
How does KV cache persistence interact with cudagraph replay?
Can we get deterministic kernel path selection across restarts?
What are recommended quant profiles for our 7B family model?
transcript:
00:00:12 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): okay hey everyone thanks for hopping on, uh let's do quick intros then jump into the traces we saw yesterday.
00:00:25 Speaker 2 (Eve): hey all, Eve here, ML eng on the recommender, we've been seeing these weird tail spikes with our 7B variants when switching from hosted to our private cluster.
00:00:38 Speaker 3 (Maya): yeah those spikes looked like cudagraph replay hiccups more than just batch cold starts, we pulled the NVTX and there were some unexpected syncs.
00:00:52 Speaker 3 (Maya): Diego, you wanna highlight the kernel map?
00:01:00 Speaker 4 (Diego): sure, so in tensorrt-llm path we see fused attention kernels get selected for token lengths under 1024, but when sequence mix moves to short+long the runtime flips to an unfused matmul path, causing a kernel switch mid-request which can blow up the latency tail.
00:01:22 Speaker 2 (Eve): right and we noticed that on our end too, sometimes it looks like the KV cache is evicted and then a follow-up request rehydrates it, but with cudagraphs replayed it does a sync wait.
00:01:37 Speaker 5 (Marcus): sorry quick q — when you say evicted is that NVMe swap or GPU-side KV eviction?
00:01:44 Speaker 4 (Diego): primarily GPU-side LRU eviction in our measurement; when the batch packing tries to co-locate many prefixes the KV capacity gets pressure and older entries are evicted. The eviction plus cudagraph replay ordering sometimes forces a blocking memcpy.
00:02:02 Speaker 2 (Eve): that matches our logs. Also noticed a difference between tensorrt-llm builds from vendor and what v-llm does: v-llm tends to keep a persistent per-session cache and reuses smaller kernels but has less fused op coverage, so latency median is okay but p99...
00:02:22 Speaker 3 (Maya): exactly, vLLM's path avoids some of the heavy fusion so it's more stable but not as throughput optimal. Tensorrt-llm gives higher tokens/sec but with these kernel-path flips p95/p99 suffer.
00:02:40 Speaker 6 (Priya): is that something we can control with scheduling? like pin model shards or fix an execution path?
00:02:47 Speaker 4 (Diego): there are heuristics — kernel selection is influenced by sequence length histograms, quant profile, and whether cudagraphs are enabled. One lever is forcing a fixed kernel path by constraining max sequence at capture time, but that's not always acceptable for your mixed prompt distribution.
00:03:06 Speaker 2 (Eve): hmm and what about nonblocking cudagraph replay? We tried enabling nonblocking replay to avoid stalls but saw sporadic out-of-order timings.
00:03:16 Speaker 3 (Maya): nonblocking helps throughput but can introduce subtle ordering issues if your KV cache rehydration hasn't completed. We've seen race windows where the replayed graph assumes KV present and issues kernels that then wait on implicit syncs, which surface as tail spikes.
00:03:33 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): Tom, you joined a bit late, any high-level constraints we should keep in mind for private deployment?
00:03:40 Speaker 7 (Tom): main constraints: strict data residency, SSO/SAML integration, and we need predictable p99 < 300ms for 32-token prompts at 50 qps. Also limited to 2 x A100s per node for budget reasons.
00:03:58 Speaker 4 (Diego): 2xA100 is fine, but NVLink and numa placement matter — if the RDMA path isn't pinned we saw extra cross-socket memcpy that exacerbates cudagraph syncs.
00:04:13 Speaker 5 (Marcus): ok so concretely what should we run on our side to reproduce?
00:04:18 Speaker 3 (Maya): we'd like a traffic replay with representative prompt length distribution (short: 70%, mid: 25%, long: 5%), plus the model artifact and quant profile you used. Also enable trace level 3 for cudagraph replay logs.
00:04:34 Speaker 2 (Eve): we can do that. One thing: our infra team uses an older CUDA stack (11.8) right now — is that a blocker for tensorrt-llm features?
00:04:45 Speaker 4 (Diego): there are features in cuda 12+ that help with more deterministic cudagraph replay and improved kernel selection APIs. TensorRT optimizations also expect cuda 12 for some fused kernels. We can run compatibility tests but recommend upgrading if possible.
00:05:01 Speaker 6 (Priya): upgrade path is nontrivial, multi-team approvals required. Could Redwood provide a compatibility matrix and a minimal repro that works on 11.8?
00:05:10 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): yes we'll share a compatibility doc and a minimal repro script.
00:05:15 Speaker 2 (Eve): on quantization — we tried int8 and saw minor quality drift, int4 was much worse for our recommendation task. Do you have recommended int8 profiles?
00:05:25 Speaker 3 (Maya): int8 can work well if you use per-channel calibration and avoid aggressive weight-only quant for attention projection layers. We'll run a quick sensitivity run on a sample of your eval set. Diego will own that.
00:05:38 Speaker 4 (Diego): noted — I'll run a 2-point int8 vs fp16 eval and share delta.
00:05:44 Speaker 5 (Marcus): one more infra concern: our VPC has strict MTU and we sometimes see fragmentation on gRPC requests to the host agent. Could that interact with your batching logic?
00:05:55 Speaker 3 (Maya): batching is internal to the device runtime and shouldn't depend on MTU, but the host->agent RPCs that assemble requests and KV lookup metadata can get delayed. If your controlplane agent is on a different subnet, that adds jitter before the request hits the device queue which then amplifies p99. Pinning the agent co-located with GPU process helps.
00:06:16 Speaker 2 (Eve): okay, good point. We'll test colocating agent and model process.
00:06:22 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): let's walk through the traces you sent — we annotated NVTX and found two patterns: a) bulk kernel swap at ~150ms into the capture, b) a blocking memcpy on KV rehydrate at ~312ms. Maya can you explain how the graph capture exposes that?
00:06:38 Speaker 3 (Maya): graph capture records the sequence of kernels; when the capture sees a blocking memcpy it bakes that into the graph ordering. On replay, if the memcpy is now nonblocking (because of changed memory residency) you can still hit a race where kernels assume data present and then stall; conversely if the memcpy is newly blocking it becomes a serialized point. The variability across runs then shows up as p99 volatility.
00:06:58 Speaker 2 (Eve): that explains the nondeterminism we saw across node restarts.
00:07:02 Speaker 5 (Marcus): is there a way to force cudagraph to re-evaluate at runtime? like force a capture per N requests?
00:07:10 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes, capture windows and fallbacks are configuration knobs — you can capture per sequence-length bucket and fallback to eager execution on mismatch. That reduces raw throughput but improves stability. Redwood's runtime has a policy to auto-capture on stable histograms and auto-fallback after X failures.
00:07:27 Speaker 6 (Priya): what's the recommended X for production?
00:07:30 Speaker 3 (Maya): we recommend capture stability threshold at 10k requests per bucket and fallback after 3 consecutive graph errors, but for your mixed load we might lower to 2 errors and add a short cooldown.
00:07:46 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): action item: share our recommended config and a small script to simulate mixed prompts.
00:07:52 Speaker 2 (Eve): cool. Also, we saw that when we enable aggressive batching the KV cache occupancy grows and causes eviction earlier; any advice there?
00:08:03 Speaker 4 (Diego): tradeoff: larger batches = better throughput, more prefetched KV per request = more memory pressure. For your 2xA100 we recommend a batch budget that keeps peak KV usage below 70% of GPU cache footprint. We can help calculate that from your model's KV per token metric.
00:08:20 Speaker 5 (Marcus): what's KV per token roughly for our 7B?
00:08:23 Speaker 3 (Maya): roughly 0.9-1.2MB per token depending on key/value layout and quantization. If you quantize KV to int8 you can reduce footprint but watch accuracy.
00:08:35 Speaker 6 (Priya): Diego, can you run that quant-sens test and also output expected p50/p95/p99 at two batch sizes?
00:08:42 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes, will include that in the artifact.
00:08:47 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): final topic — deterministic kernel selection across restarts. We can't fully guarantee identical kernels because driver heuristics and small timing differences can sway selection. But we can make it robust: 1) use fixed capture parameters, 2) use forced kernel hints in the runtime, 3) provide an operator guide to pin affinities and ensure cuda/driver versions aligned.
00:09:12 Speaker 7 (Tom): good, that gives us something actionable.
00:09:16 Speaker 2 (Eve): are there known issues with specific TensorRT versions and our pattern?
00:09:20 Speaker 3 (Maya): some older TRT builds used different heuristics for multi-head attention tiling; we saw a few regressions pre-8.x. We'll list tested versions in the compatibility doc.
00:09:31 Speaker 5 (Marcus): can Redwood run a short on-prem pilot with node spec we provide?
00:09:35 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): yes — pilot plan: 2-day baseline run with your traffic replay, kernel NVTX + cudagraph traces, and quant sensitivity. We'll do a joint run and then a follow-up to tune capture/fallback config.
00:09:50 Speaker 2 (Eve): perfect. One last thing — we've seen ModelServeCo claim they avoid these graph races by not using cudagraphs. Is that a viable strategy?
00:09:59 Speaker 3 (Maya): you can avoid cudagraphs and run eager kernels; that's more deterministic but you'll lose a lot of throughput. For some latency‑sensitive use cases eager can be better, but you'd need more GPU capacity. It's a cost vs stability tradeoff.
00:10:15 Speaker 4 (Diego): also note some cudagraph implementations in the wild are brittle; our runtime has a hybrid mode where hot paths use graphs and fallback to eager for off‑pattern sequences. That tends to hit the sweet spot.
00:10:29 Speaker 7 (Tom): ok that sounds reasonable. Let's get the artifacts exchanged.
00:10:33 Speaker 1 (Sanjay): recap of next steps: Maya to upload NVTX traces and how-to, Diego to run quant test and share p-metrics, Catalyst to provide traffic replay and node spec. We'll reconvene after pilot scheduling.
00:10:48 Speaker 2 (Eve): thanks everyone.
00:10:50 Speaker 3 (Maya): thanks, wrapping up.
00:10:55 [meeting ends, recording stopped]
